claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure.
The hierarchical heterostructure consists of nanoscale secondary phases or precipitates integrated within a microscale grain/matrix architecture.
Experimentally measurable descriptors such as precipitate size, precipitate distribution, and grain-boundary characteristics can serve as inputs to a physics-informed multiscale reduced-order model.
The hierarchical heterostructure provides a scale-bridging mechanism that decouples elastic responses at atomistic or nanoscale levels from plastic and fracture responses at the microscale.
The hierarchical heterostructure modulates load transfer.
The hierarchical heterostructure modulates crack propagation.
The nanoscale features are stiffer than the surrounding matrix.
The matrix is more ductile than the nanoscale features.
Load transfer between stiff nanoscale features and the more ductile matrix governs part of the mechanical response.
Property gradients in the hierarchical structure can be used to predict elastic response.
Critical stress concentrations captured by the model drive yielding and fracture.
Scale decoupling permits a reduced-order description that bypasses computationally expensive full-physics simulations.
The proposed model can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior more accurately than established full-physics simulation approaches.
The proposed model can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior more rapidly than established full-physics simulation approaches.
The proposed model is expected to reduce simulation time by roughly 50% relative to conventional full-scale simulations.
The proposed model is expected to improve predictive accuracy for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture parameters by an estimated 10–20% relative to conventional full-scale simulations.
Established full-physics atomistic and continuum simulations require intensive computational resources.
Established simulations struggle to capture accurately the contribution of multiscale heterogeneity to mechanical response.
Significant evolution of the heterostructure during testing can invalidate the fixed microstructural descriptors and cause the model to fail.
Emergent interactions between phases that cannot be represented through scale decoupling can cause the model to fail.
